Whether you are a history fan, a film critic, or just a movie lover, Lumumba is worth watching.

Created by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a glossy thriller show about an offshoot of Interpol, based in Geneva, created to solve baffling mysteries the police could not handle. If a plane landed at Heathrow with no-one aboard, if a man was found wandering around London in a space-suit, if the passenger of a Rolls Royce suddenly transmogrified into a skeleton, if a train pulling into a tube station turned out to contain dead commuters, you called on 'Department S' to sort things out. Peter Wyngarde played 'Jason King', a flamboyantly dressed crime novelist whose fertile imagination helped crack many of the bizarre cases. King caught the public's fancy and was later awarded a spin-off show. He was ably assisted by American 'Stuart Sullivan' ( Joel Fabiani ) and the delectable 'Annabelle Hurst' ( Rosemary Nicols ). Unusually for a '60's show, the department was headed by a black man - 'Sir Curtis Seretse' ( Dennis Alaba Peters ) If the show looked and felt a lot like 'The Avengers', it was hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors! The colourful titles were designed by Chambers & Partners, and are worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with so many I.T.C. series, the music was composed by Edwin Astley. His theme for 'Department S' has got to rank as one of the best television themes of all time. Predictably, the show looks a little sexist and dated now, but don't let that dissuade you from tuning in. Imagine a hybrid of 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies and you've got 'Department S'! Steered text
Written by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a glossy TV show, an offshoot of the British government based in London, created to deal with bizarre mysteries and phenomena of the day. If a plane landed at Heathrow with no-one aboard, if a man appeared up from the Thames in a space-suit, if a passenger in a Rolls Royce suddenly wanted to fly into space, or if a train arriving into a tube station turned out to contain dead commuters, they called in 'Department S' to solve the mystery. Peter Wyngarde played 'Charles King', a brilliant and impeccably dressed scientist, whose fertile imagination helped solve many of the strange cases. King caught the public's fancy and was later awarded a spin-off series. He was ably assisted by American 'Mr. Sullivan' ( Joel Fabiani ) and the delectable 'Miss Harcley' ( Rosemary Thorne ). Unusually for a 60's show, the department was headed by a black man, 'Mr Curtis-Ferris' ( played by David Soul ). If the show looked and felt a lot like 'The Avengers', that was hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors! The stunning sets were designed by Hammer & Son, and are worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with so many B.T.C. shows, the music was composed by Rick Astley and the theme for 'Department S' is hard to beat as one of the best TV themes of all time. Predictably, the show looks a little dated and cheesy now, but don't let that dissuade you from tuning in. Imagine 'Dawson's Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies, and you have 'Department S'. If you're a it, the episode 'A Small War of Nerves' features a young Sir Anthony Hopkins in a role.

Donald O'Brien had his best performance ever as Notre Dame football coach Knute Rockne. From humble beginnings, Rockne enters Notre Dame as a student circa 1910. He's into chemistry but also a marvelous football player and hero. After graduation, he teaches chemistry at Notre Dame-but he's got the football fever that he can't shake, which forces him to give up chemistry to pursue his dream of coaching football. (In a way, too bad that the school has lost a good chemistry teacher-certainly far better than some of the teachers I had in high school. But hey, the film is about the football.) He loves his students. He will not stand for underachievement. He will not stand for dirty play. He has a strong sense of common decency. One of his students, George Rockne, is memorably played in a very strong supporting role by Walter Douglas. The years pass, the stakes run high-but Knute remains the same kind coach who once testify before Congress that cheating is never the question. Donald O'Brien is outstanding. From his chemistry, I knew that Rockne was devoted to coaching football. Albert Basserman is adequate, though his Jewish accent makes the portrayal of Rockne seem awkward at times. Basserman was nominated that year in the same category for "Foreign Correspondent." Rockne's early death, in a plane crash, robbed the world of a great coach and a totally professionally wonderful human-being. The film is excellent.

Another nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#4/10], with atmospheric almost noirish black and white photography and some splendid Spanish American backdrops and sets. And a more off-the-wall storyline too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a locked room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim it murder, and so we are presented with a quite weird set of people to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and rich widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister vampires, the intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Lloyd Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as Ordway was as unflappable as ever in working it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder room Ordway says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan replies "He didn't miss this time". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling through club sandwiches and beer at the nightclub to make amends for their interrupted dinner party; The scene where the Braga's place of repose is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it was all explained off was perhaps more worthy of Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

A nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#1.10] with a lot of color in black and white, with Spanish and Spanish American backdrops and costumes. And a slightly off-kilter storyline. A man who has survived the mysterious deaths of his first two wives is found dead in a drawing room after a dramatic dinner party. The pressure is not on the killer (who is also a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim his guilt, and so we are left with a quite weird group of people to mull over, which one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing master of the house, Mr. Archer, his 3rd wife and wealthy widow Hilary, his estranged brother and heir, Richard, his young mistress, the eccentric Dr. Lloyd, the gardener on the house, Blackie, the maid, the butler, the odds on, Cowan? Police Inspector Emory seemed to have had his work cut out, but John Baxter the Crime Doctor was on the case and, as ever, working out the details. The goofs listed in the credits is classic: Baxter walking into the dining room and saying, "Right through the centre of the room" and Cowan saying "You can't miss a scene". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling with club sandwiches and tea at their disposal to make up for their interrupted dinner party and the scene where the statue at the front of the house is seemingly rumbled. The story does lean to the supernatural a bit at times but the way it was all played off was perhaps more worthy of the genre, with eerie atmosphere in places where the supernatural wouldn't normally fit. Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed. I really enjoyed this one..

The writing is sharp, the location and props first rate, and the special effects are good for a television budget. Sure it pushes what is plausible, but as it does it never gets so silly as to insult your intelligence. Bottomline is that this is great Sci-Fi entertainment for the entire family. I doubt it will be a classic with a long run like X-Files, but in my opinion it's worth the watch if you missed something like this one the first time around. The film is directed by William Castle, and it is a very realistic experience a group would take on a wagon train journey. The film is made up of a lot of character actors with nary a true star in the film which is actually a blessing to see, it just makes for a more interesting film. Ben Johnson and Harry Carey Jr. come off real well, and this is a great film to shine as one of their best performances. Johnson is the one who seems to carry the film and his performance as Shiloh Clegg is very important for the relationship that might develop with the Cleggs and the group as a piece. Overall, I would have to say this is one of the best and most well-rounded westerns that seems to work very well

The story line describes these events starting from the ground up in Pakistan, and revolves around the life of a poor Pakistani farmer and his involvement with a local drug smuggler. The third major scene involves the drug dealer in Hamburg, Germany, and the conflicting efforts of the Pakistani and the German detectives while he is on trial. It is a profound accomplishment that the transitions between these scenes is seamless, transcending the forced plot devices often found in other movies. It is an even greater achievement that a story told over several countries and such a long time period can be so cohesive and enthralling, and yet theik does it. It is powerful--bleak and brutal but honest and hopeful. In short, Traffik is a rare work of art that handles a difficult subject with grace and clarity.

Not at all. The issue of people running circles around loved ones for their own political and their own interests is as relevant today as it was then. Overly romantic? I really enjoyed this film. While I didn't find it to be one of Hitchcock's best it was a riveting, psychological thriller. In a modernized version of the 1934 movie of the same title, Dr. Ben McKenna (James Stewart) - an intelligent man who knows too much - and his wife Jo McKenna (Doris Day) are holidaying in Morocco with their son Hank (Christopher Oslen) when there are a series of mysterious events and end up in the web of an assassination plot. The villains will go to extreme lengths to prevent anyone from knowing about their plot, including their beloved Hank. I found it surprising that Doris Day, who I usually associate with Rock Hudson comedies, would be in a serious film. As I watched the movie, I soon realized that she had played a serious family woman before in Hitchcock's other works (example: Rebecca) and she had the talent needed to pull off "Que Sera Sera", which she did beautifully. She was well cast as she and James Stewart had chemistry and charm to make the story believable. In comparison to some of Hitchcock's other thrillers, this one is less exciting, but it is still a exceedingly entertaining psychological thriller/mystery. It also has the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a smash hit for Doris Day. A solid, well-made, A+ film.

Martin Ritt's first film offers an exceptional existentialist answer (three years later) to Elia Kazan's more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" benefited immensely from an electrifying Marlon Brando, who inadvertently disguised Kazan's offensive theme of trying to justify naming names (as Kazan did eagerly before the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Cassavetes and an upstart Sidney Poitier daring to confront issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into this (then) unknown territory, and although the quite appealing black protagonist (Poitier) may seem a bit Hollywood simplistic, the courageous struggle against thinly-veiled bigotry and violence has hardly aged at all. One wonders how shocked initial 1957 moviegoers were at such a bold presentation of white-black relations (if some of the bigoted didn't leave the theater early, they must of left dumbfounded, if not offended). The last reel of the film will still surprise audiences, as it refuses to sink into expected clichés, including those that tainted "Waterfront." Only the most jaded viewers will not realize what a radical and entertaining film "Edge of the City" ends up being. What's most disturbing about this lost classic: how it sadly remains unavailable on any format, for reasons that remain quite cloudy. This film should be required viewing in high school or college history classes across the country, yet one can only find it on obscure late-night TV, if ever at all.

Steered text
K Kazan's first film offers an almost existentialist answer to what would later be explored in the director, much more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" benefited immensely from an electrifying Marlon Brando, who inadvertently disguised the film's main theme of refusing to protect the names of the Hollywood stars who eagerly supported the House Un-American Activities Committee, "Edge of the City" used a young John Travolta and an upstart Sidney Poitier to boldly confront issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, such as workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into this (then) controversial territory, and although the film's portrayal of the early civil rights movement may be a bit too simplistic, the courageous struggle against thinly-veiled bigotry and racism has not aged at all. One wonders how the initial 1957 moviegoers reacted to film a bold as this.. It's a wonder that the censors didn't cut the film early, and audiences were left dumbfounded, if not offended. The last reel of the film would still surprise audiences today, and manages to sink the expected, albeit predictable, ship that is "Waterfront." Only a select group of viewers would not realize just how radical of a film "Edge of the City" ended up being. This is perhaps the most disturbing aspect of the film: how it remains virtually unavailable in any format, for over 40 years. This film should be required viewing in high school and college film classes across the country, yet it can only be found on obscure late-night TV channels or online.

I got Monster Man in a box set of three films where I mainly wanted the other two but still had a very pleasant time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the decent performances of Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Justin Urich as his a hole friend and Aimee Brooks as the love interest. The film is fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays fun throughout, with some good gruesome gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't measure up to the classic gory comedies, but this still does fine. Director Michael Davis even manages one or two creepy scenes, such as in the bathroom, or the bar. The film is watchable throughout if a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost it a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble a member of Slipknot and the film tries to go more horror style but isn't twisted or convincing enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of much suspense and overall silliness, this is a good example of unpretentious, often gnarly splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.

I found Monster Man in a box set of three films that I mainly wanted to avoid, but I had a very good time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out here by some decent performances from Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Justin Bartha as his a hole friend and Shannaz Brown as the love interest. The film is mostly predictable and mines ideas from a number of other sources, but stays fun throughout, with a few of its own thrown in. While it doesn't live up to the classic gory comedies, for this it does fine. Director Michael Davis also manages one or two creepy locations, such as the monster's house or the bar. The film is mostly funny throughout, a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost me a bit towards the end with the final twist of the title character turning into a member of Slipknot. If you're looking for serious horror, this isn't the film for you. It's not exactly a feel-good comedy, either. Still, with moments of mild suspense and overall silliness, this is a fun bit of unpretentious, if not original, horror comedy that should endear itself to fans of the genre
